## Overview

**Goal:** Create a new branch in your repository, make a change on that
branch, and merge it back into `main` using a pull request.

A **branch** is a copy of your repository where you can make changes
without affecting the `main` branch. This lets you try things out or work
on a new piece of analysis, then bring the changes back in once you're
happy with them.

This exercise uses the repository you created in
`Exercise_GitHub_Setup.Rmd`, entirely through the web browser at
[https://github.com](https://github.com).

Written by Claude with GitHub Copilot.

---

## Step 1 — Create a New Branch

1. Go to your repository's main page
2. Click the branch dropdown, currently showing **main** (top-left, above
   the file list)
3. Type a new branch name, e.g. `add-notes`
4. Click **Create branch: add-notes from 'main'**

> ✅ **Checkpoint:** The branch dropdown now shows `add-notes` instead of
> `main`. You are now working on your new branch.

---

## Step 2 — Make a Change on the Branch

1. While still on the `add-notes` branch, click on `README.md`
2. Click the **pencil icon** (✏️) to edit the file
3. Add a new line at the bottom, e.g.:

```
## Notes
This is a test edit made on the add-notes branch.
```

4. Scroll down to **Commit changes**
5. Write a commit message, e.g. `Add notes section`
6. Select **Commit directly to the `add-notes` branch** (this option
   appears because you are no longer on `main`)
7. Click **Commit changes**

> ✅ **Checkpoint:** Your edit is saved on `add-notes`. If you switch the
> branch dropdown back to `main`, the change will **not** be there — it
> only exists on `add-notes` so far.

---

## Step 3 — Open a Pull Request

A **pull request (PR)** proposes merging your branch's changes into
`main`.

1. GitHub often shows a banner: *"add-notes had recent pushes"* with a
   **Compare & pull request** button — click it. (If you don't see the
   banner, click the **Pull requests** tab → **New pull request**, and
   set base = `main`, compare = `add-notes`.)
2. Add a title and short description of what you changed
3. Click **Create pull request**

> ✅ **Checkpoint:** You should see a pull request page showing the diff
> (the lines added/removed) between `add-notes` and `main`.

---

## Step 4 — Merge the Pull Request

1. On the pull request page, scroll down and click **Merge pull request**
2. Click **Confirm merge**
3. (Optional) Click **Delete branch** to clean up `add-notes` now that its
   changes are in `main`

> ✅ **Checkpoint:** Switch the branch dropdown to `main` and open
> `README.md` — your notes section should now appear there.

---

## Why Bother With Branches?

For solo work on small files, committing directly to `main` (as in the
setup exercise) is fine. Branches become useful when you want to:

- Try an analysis without risking your working `main` version
- Keep `main` clean and functional while experimenting
- Collaborate with others without overwriting each other's work

---

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Solution |
|---|---|
| Don't see the branch dropdown | Make sure you're on the repository's main **Code** page, not inside a file. |
| No "Compare & pull request" banner appears | Go to the **Pull requests** tab → **New pull request** and manually select `main` and `add-notes`. |
| **Merge pull request** button is greyed out or shows a conflict | This means the same lines were changed on both branches. For this simple exercise, that shouldn't happen — ask for help if it does. |
| Accidentally committed to `main` instead of the branch | Double-check the branch dropdown before editing next time. You can still create a branch afterward and continue from there. |

---

## Conclusion

You now know how to isolate changes on a branch and bring them into
`main` via a pull request — the basic workflow behind most collaborative
work on GitHub.
